rv.q: It is the real thing—a traditional, fantastical Broadway show—independent of both the animated film and the 1956 film with Ingrid Bergman, which are said to have “inspired” it.
But now the secret can be told: Anastasia is the richest and fullest family show to hit Broadway in years.
In this alt-reality, history is rewritten, a princess finds her bliss — and an old-fashioned musical likely lives happy ever after.
Sumptuous production values and a fine cast cannot, in the end, overcome the drawbacks of the production.
Anastasia is undeniably entertaining, but also relevant to the magical thinking that seems to have overtaken so much of the world.
It’s kitschy, old-fashioned entertainment given a relatively sophisticated presentation, and you have to acknowledge its success when you hear the target demographic swoon on cue.
What 'Anastasia' offers instead is a procession of lovely pictures, enough to compensate for a book that doesn't delve nearly deeply enough into the search for identity that is at the musical's core.
The lyrics are self-explanatory (“she trembles like a flower, but in her is a power”) and the songs (one sounds like “Officer Krupke”) are familiar.

But once Terrence McNally's book finds its feet, and the physical production gets out of the way of the several gorgeous, old-school ballads therein (including, of course, "Journey to the Past," superbly rendered by Altomare), "Anastasia" has its moments of credible emancipation.
The show in which she appears trembles nonstop with internal conflicts during its drawn-out two-and-a-half hours.
You can’t have your revolution and eat it too.
It’s less a cabinet of wonders than a featureless box.
It may have taken 20 years for "Anastasia" to make its way from the screen to the stage, but this journey to the past has proven to be well worth the wait.
So Anastasia sends you, if you let yourself be sent, off on a cascade of melody and visual splendor.

If you are particular about Russian political and cultural history, you might want to be gripping a stress ball before taking your seat at the musical Anastasia on Broadway. If you want to watch a proudly old-school Broadway musical with the best snow effects ever (thank you, projection designer Aaron Rhyne), however, then no stress balls needed.
Twenty years later, it's a fidget-inducing, two-and-a-half-hour Broadway musical, with a production not nearly animated enough to warrant that running time.
Christy Altomare is smashing as Anya, with powerhouse vocals full of spark and sensitive yearning.
Anastasia is surprisingly mild.
For the rest of us, however, it doesn’t live up to the hype.
The show, despite being filled with some very good songs and performances, suffers from its own identity crisis.
As the two lovers, Christy Altomare and Derek Klena display pretty singing voices, and otherwise show as much depth as the animated-film characters their roles are based on.
The Oscar-nominated hit from the original movie, Journey to the Past, as well as Once Upon a December are the stand-outs here, though they've been augmented by nearly 20 new songs.
It is assured, it is lyrical, it is melodic, it is beautiful, it is dashing, it is moving and it is charming.

Perhaps inescapably, however, Anastasia nevertheless winds up promoting nostalgia for the last reign of the Romanovs, those elegantly attired autocrats who sponsored pogroms against the Jews and violently suppressed popular Russian calls for democracy.
I just can't pretend that what's actually happened, you know, real people getting murdered, didn't happen and it's all ok.
